identity.title: MetaEmbed: Scaling Multimodal Retrieval at Test-Time with Flexible Late Interaction

problem.claim: Design multimodal retrieval embeddings that retain fine-grained expressiveness while remaining efficient for large-scale multi-vector retrieval.

gap.claim: Existing approaches either compress queries and candidates into one potentially limiting vector or generate too many vectors for cost-effective retrieval.

contributions.claim: MetaEmbed appends a fixed number of learnable Meta Tokens during training and uses their contextualized final-layer representations as compact multi-vector embeddings at test time.
Matryoshka Multi-Vector Retrieval training organizes information by granularity across the vectors.
The framework supports test-time selection of the number of indexed and interacting tokens, allowing a quality–efficiency tradeoff.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present MetaEmbed as a new framework that rethinks multimodal embedding construction and interaction at scale.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report state-of-the-art retrieval performance on MMEB and ViDoRe.
The authors report robust scaling to models with 32B parameters on those evaluations.

narrative_sequence.summary: Multimodal embeddings capture query–candidate relevance, but single-vector and high-vector-count designs expose expressiveness or efficiency limitations.
MetaEmbed introduces learnable Meta Tokens whose contextualized representations become compact multi-vector embeddings.
Matryoshka training organizes information by granularity, enabling users to vary token counts at test time to balance quality and efficiency.
The authors report state-of-the-art benchmark retrieval and scaling to 32B-parameter models.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links variable token counts at test time with an explicit retrieval-quality versus efficiency tradeoff, supported by training that organizes information by granularity.

lessons.interpretation: A controllable inference budget can make one retrieval representation adaptable to different deployment constraints.
lessons.application: When designing scalable retrieval, train representations so prefixes or subsets of components correspond to progressively finer information, then expose that budget as an inference-time control.
lessons.exception: This is unsuitable when downstream retrieval requires a fixed representation or when partial components do not preserve meaningful granularity.

unknowns: The abstract does not report metrics, baseline identities, dataset sizes, or the specific conditions underlying the state-of-the-art and robustness claims.
It does not quantify the quality–efficiency tradeoff across different token counts or explain the training objective in detail.
The abstract alone does not establish independent validity, reproducibility, or priority of the stated contributions.
